title: CMP 62 15 cassava (PSB Cv 13): Yield, Maturity and Characteristics
metaTitle: CMP 62 15 cassava: Yield, Maturity and Characteristics
metaDescription: CMP 62 15 cassava is a cassava variety. 10 to 12 months to harvest, 30.4 t/ha in trials. See its pest ratings and traits.
excerpt: CMP 62 15 is a registered cassava variety, also sold or known as PSB Cv 13. It was registered with the National Seed Industry Council (NSIC) in 1997 as NSIC 1997 Cv 13. It takes 10 to 12 months from planting to harvest, with 30.4 tonnes per hectare on average in the trials.

blocks.text: If you came here looking for PSB Cv 13, this is the same cassava. The facts below come from the NSIC registry kept by the Bureau of Plant Industry. Compare it with the others in our [cassava variety finder](/crop-varieties/cassava), or see [every crop variety](/crop-varieties) we list. For the crop itself, read our guide: [Land preparation for root crops](/land-preparation/root-crop-land-preparation).

items: **Days to harvest:** 10 to 12 months from planting to harvest.
**Yield:** 30.4 tonnes per hectare on average in the trials.

blocks.text: How long does it take, and how much does it yield?

CMP 62 15 cassava takes 10 to 12 months from planting to harvest. That is about the average of the 42 cassava varieties with a day count, 10.5 months. Count the months from planting, and plan the harvest for a dry stretch when you can.

Its average yield of 30.4 t/ha trails the average of its group, 32.38. Trial yields come from well managed plots, so your own will depend on water, fertilizer, pests and timing.

Once you know the day count, anee.io dates every task from each lot's own planting day, with [the growth stages and weather](/features/growth-stages-and-weather) beside it.
Is it resistant to pests and diseases?

blocks.caption: Reactions in the registry trials, rated under natural field conditions
rows: Took some damage but held up
Took some damage but held up

blocks.text: It showed no weak spot in the ratings on record. Still, a resistant variety can break down when a new strain or pest population comes, so keep scouting.

The pests and diseases that hit cassava fields most often: [whitefly](/pests/whitefly), [anthracnose](/diseases/anthracnose), [Cercospora leaf spot](/diseases/cercospora-leaf-spot), [mealybug](/pests/mealybug). Our [pest finder](/pests) and [disease finder](/diseases) help you name what you see.

Its roots have white flesh and cream skin. Dry matter is 34.8 percent. A higher dry matter cooks mealy and gives processors more flour or starch from each tonne. The starch content is 22.8 percent. Its cyanide level, the HCN content, is low. A low level is safer for the table, while a high level calls for peeling, soaking and full cooking. It is recommended for processing (food, feeds, starch).
Where and when to plant CMP 62 15 cassava

The registry recommends it for anywhere in the country. Pick by buyer first. Starch and feed plants pay for yield and starch content, while the table wants a sweet, low cyanide variety that boils soft. A high starch variety needs a buyer within a day of harvest, because the roots spoil fast.

Ask your municipal agriculturist or nearby farmers how it did in your area last season.
Try it on a small area first, beside the variety you usually plant, before you switch the whole farm.

items.q: Is PSB Cv 13 the same as CMP 62 15?
items.a: Yes. PSB Cv 13 is another name for CMP 62 15, registered as NSIC 1997 Cv 13. Seed sellers use both, so ask for either one.

items.q: How long does it take to harvest?
items.a: It takes 10 to 12 months from planting to harvest. Then the weather and your care decide the exact day.
The record shows 30.4 tonnes per hectare on average in the trials. Your own yield depends on the soil, water, fertilizer and pests on your farm.
The registry recommends it for anywhere in the country. Ask your municipal agriculturist how it has done in your town.

items.q: Where can I buy seed of CMP 62 15?
items.a: Ask an accredited seed dealer in your province, the seller named on this page or your municipal agriculturist. Look for the certified seed tag or a sealed pack before you pay.
